segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this reason I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: if indeed you have heard of the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: by revelation the secret was made known to me, as I have already written briefly,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and in reading it you can perceive my insight into the secret of Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: which in other generations was not made known to the sons of men as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow sharers in the promise in Christ Jesus through the good news,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: of which I became a servant according to the gift of God’s grace that was given to me according to the working of his power—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to me, less than the least of all the holy ones, this grace was given—to bring the Gentiles the good news of the unfathomable riches of Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to enlighten everyone about the plan of the secret hidden for ages in God, who created all things,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that now, through the assembly, the many-sided wisdom of God might be made known to the rulers and the authorities in the heavenly places,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: according to the purpose of the ages that he carried out in Christ Jesus our Lord,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through faith in him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So I ask you not to lose heart over my afflictions on your behalf, which are your glory.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this reason I bend my knees before the Father,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: from whom every family in the heavens and on earth takes its name,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, so that you, rooted and grounded in love,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: may have the strength to comprehend, with all the holy ones, what is the breadth and length and height and depth,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, so that you may be filled to all the fullness of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now to him who is able to do beyond everything, far more than we ask or imagine, according to the power at work in us,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to him be the glory in the assembly and in Christ Jesus to all generations, forever and ever. Amen.

notes.note: The sentence breaks off here without a verb. Paul digresses in verses 2–13 to explain his commission, then takes up the thought again in verse 14 with the same words, “For this reason.” Some translations supply a verb such as “am” or “pray” in verse 1; this one leaves the break visible, as the Greek does.

The Greek word is the ordinary plural for “nations” or “peoples.” In Jewish usage it meant the non-Jewish peoples, and that is its sense throughout this chapter. Elsewhere in this translation the same word appears as “nations” when peoples as such are meant.

Most English versions keep “mystery,” treating it as a technical term for a truth once hidden and now revealed. In Jewish Greek of the period the word was the ordinary term for a secret, especially a plan of God that only he can disclose. “Mystery” now suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, whereas Paul’s point is that the secret has been told and can be stated plainly, as verse 6 does.

The traditional rendering is “gospel,” which now sounds like a religious term or the title of a book. The Greek was an everyday word for the announcement of good news, including public proclamations. The related verb in verse 8 is rendered with the same phrase.

Many translations have “saints”; others use “God’s people.” The word refers to all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue, which is not the sense.

notes.traditional: fellowship (KJV, following a different Greek reading); administration; plan
notes.note: This is the same Greek word rendered “stewardship” in verse 2. It covers both the management entrusted to a steward and the arrangement by which something is managed. In verse 2 Paul’s own commission is in view; here most interpreters take it as God’s arrangement for carrying out the secret. Some translations use “administration” in both places.

“Church” is the near-universal rendering, and readers know what it refers to. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Septuagint’s term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” wherever the Greek word occurs.

notes.traditional: by the faith of him; through faith in him
notes.note: The Greek is literally “through the faith of him.” The majority reading takes this as the believer’s faith in Christ. A substantial minority of scholars read it as Christ’s own faithfulness: “through his faithfulness.” The grammar allows either.

notes.phrase: I ask you not to lose heart
notes.traditional: I desire that ye faint not
notes.note: The Greek states neither whom Paul is asking nor who might lose heart. Most translations take it as a request to the readers not to be discouraged by his imprisonment. It could also be a prayer to God, either that the readers not lose heart or, less probably, that Paul himself not lose heart.

Older versions have “tribulations” here; modern ones often have “sufferings.” The Greek is an ordinary word for hardship that presses on a person. “Tribulation” is now widely heard as the name of a specific end-time period, which says more than the word does.

The Greek word for “family” here means a clan or lineage descended from one father, and it is formed from the word for “father.” A Greek hearer therefore caught a link between “Father” and “family” that English cannot reproduce. The older rendering “the whole family” is grammatically less likely. “In the heavens” keeps the Greek plural.

“In love” stands between two clauses in the Greek and can attach to either. Most translations, like this one, take it with what follows. The edition of the Greek text translated here punctuates it with what precedes: “that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, in love.” The original manuscripts had no punctuation, so the question is one of interpretation.

candidates.reason: Its range from a steward’s commission to God’s arrangement of history recurs in Luke 16, 1 Corinthians 9:17, Ephesians 1:10, Colossians 1:25 and 1 Timothy 1:4, and versions split among stewardship, administration, plan and dispensation.

The phrase ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις recurs five times in Ephesians and the adjective appears in John, 1 Corinthians, Philippians and Hebrews; “heavenly places,” “heavenly realms” and “the heavenlies” should not vary.
In the sense of ruling powers, paired with ἐξουσία, it recurs across Paul and elsewhere as “rulers,” “principalities” or “powers,” and needs one rendering kept distinct from ἄρχων and δύναμις.
Pervasive across the New Testament, and translators choose between “grace,” “favor” and “gift” by context; the boundaries between senses need fixing once.
A theologically loaded term in Ephesians, Colossians, John 1:16 and Romans 11, where “fullness,” “full number” and “completion” compete and consistency affects interpretation.
